problem: Source "since dinner (Mrs. Reed ... dined early)" rendered as "since lunch (Mrs. Reed dined early ...)" — the parenthesis about dining early no longer explains anything and reads as a contradiction.
new_text: There was no chance of going for a walk that day. We had wandered through the bare shrubbery for an hour that morning, but since dinner (Mrs. Reed dined early, at midday, when there were no guests), the cold winter wind had brought such dark clouds and such relentless rain that any further time outdoors was out of the question.

problem: Mrs. Reed's "contented, happy, little children" became "happy, well-behaved little children" — "contented" (the point of her reproach to Jane) is replaced by an invented "well-behaved".
new_text: Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now gathered around their mama in the drawing room. She lay on a sofa by the fire, and with her darlings around her (for the moment neither fighting nor crying), she looked perfectly content. She had excused me from joining the group, saying that she regretted having to keep me at a distance, but that until she heard from Bessie, and could see for herself, that I was genuinely trying to develop a more sociable and childlike nature, a more appealing and lively manner—something lighter, more open, more natural—she really had to exclude me from privileges meant only for contented, happy little children.

problem: The simile "I sat cross-legged, like a Turk" is dropped.
new_text: A breakfast room adjoined the drawing room, and I slipped in there. It had a bookcase, and I quickly grabbed a book, making sure it was one full of pictures. I climbed into the window seat, tucked my feet up, and sat cross-legged like a Turk. Having pulled the red curtain nearly shut, I was hidden away in double seclusion.

problem: Source "protecting, but not separating me from the drear November day" became "shielding me from but not hiding the dreary November day" — "hiding" misstates the sense (the glass protects without cutting her off) and the split construction is awkward aloud.
new_text: Folds of scarlet fabric blocked my view to the right. To the left were the clear glass panes, shielding me from the dreary November day without shutting me off from it. Now and then, while turning the pages of my book, I studied the winter afternoon. In the distance, there was nothing but a pale blur of mist and cloud. Nearby, a scene of wet lawn and battered shrubs, with endless rain sweeping wildly before a long, mournful wind.

problem: Bewick's quoted phrase "the solitary rocks and promontories" is absorbed into paraphrase ("solitary rocks and headlands"), losing its quotation marks and so the signal that Jane is quoting the book.
new_text: I went back to my book—Bewick's History of British Birds. I didn't care much for the text itself, generally speaking, but there were certain introductory pages that, young as I was, I couldn't simply skip over. They described the haunts of seabirds, "the solitary rocks and promontories" where only they lived, the coast of Norway dotted with islands from its southern tip, the Lindeness or Naze, all the way to the North Cape—

problem: The Bewick passage is presented in quotation marks but heavily reworded: "forlorn regions of dreary space" → "desolate regions of barren space", "glazed in Alpine heights" → "rising to", and "concentre the multiplied rigours of extreme cold" → "concentrate the extreme cold" ("multiplied rigours" dropped). A quotation should be only lightly modernized.
new_text: I was equally struck by the descriptions of the bleak shores of Lapland, Siberia, Spitzbergen, Nova Zembla, Iceland, Greenland, with "the vast sweep of the Arctic Zone, and those forlorn regions of dreary space—that reservoir of frost and snow, where firm fields of ice, the accumulation of centuries of winters, glazed in Alpine heights above heights, surround the pole, and concentrate the multiplied rigours of extreme cold." Of these death-white realms I formed my own idea: shadowy, like all the half-understood notions that drift through children's minds, but strangely powerful. The words in those introductory pages connected themselves to the illustrations that followed, and gave meaning to the rock standing alone in a sea of waves and spray, to the wrecked boat stranded on a desolate coast, to the cold and ghostly moon glancing through bars of cloud at a ship just sinking.

problem: "which made him bilious, and gave him a dim and bleared eye" became "left him with a sluggish look" — the digestive complaint (bilious) is replaced by an invented "sluggish look".
new_text: John Reed was a schoolboy of fourteen, four years older than me—I was only ten. He was big and heavy for his age, with a dull, unhealthy complexion, coarse features in a broad face, thick limbs, and large hands and feet. He constantly stuffed himself at meals, which made him bilious and gave him dim, bleary eyes and flabby cheeks. He should have been at school, but his mama had brought him home for a month or two on account of his "delicate health." Mr. Miles, the headmaster, said he would do perfectly well if fewer cakes and sweets were sent from home. But his mother rejected such a harsh opinion and preferred the more flattering idea that John's sallowness was due to too much studying and, perhaps, homesickness.

problem: "I was bewildered by the terror he inspired" became "his cruelty left me stunned" — the source names Jane's terror, not his cruelty, as what bewildered her.
new_text: John didn't have much affection for his mother and sisters, and he actively disliked me. He bullied and hurt me—not two or three times a week, not once or twice a day, but constantly. Every nerve in my body feared him, and every bit of me shrank when he came near. There were moments when the terror he inspired left me bewildered, because I had no defense against his threats or his violence. The servants didn't want to upset their young master by taking my side, and Mrs. Reed was blind and deaf to it all. She never saw him hit me or heard him insult me, though he did both in her very presence from time to time—more often, though, behind her back.

problem: The ironic detail "as far as he could without damaging the roots" is dropped.
new_text: As usual, I obeyed John and came up to his chair. He spent about three minutes sticking his tongue out at me as far as it would go without tearing it out at the roots. I knew he would hit me soon, and while dreading the blow, I studied the disgusting, ugly face of the person about to deliver it. I wonder if he saw that thought in my expression, because without a word, he suddenly struck me, hard. I staggered, and once I regained my balance, I stepped back a pace or two from his chair.

problem: "What a fury to fly at Master John!" became "What a terror" — "fury" (a raging creature) is the point; "terror" shifts the sense toward mischief.
new_text: "Goodness! What a fury, to fly at Master John like that!"

problem: Abbot's "think over your wickedness" softened to "think about what you've done", flattening her moralizing tone.
new_text: "No, you are less than a servant, because you do nothing to earn your keep. Now sit down and think over your wickedness."

problem: "something bad might be permitted to come down the chimney" — "permitted" (i.e. by God, following her threat of divine punishment) is dropped.
new_text: "Besides," said Miss Abbot, "God will punish her. He might strike her dead in the middle of one of her tantrums, and then where would she go? Come, Bessie, let's leave her. I wouldn't have her heart for anything. Say your prayers, Miss Eyre, when you're alone. If you don't repent, something bad might be allowed to come down the chimney and carry you off."

problem: "the spell which kept it so lonely" became "the reason it remained so lonely", losing the supernatural image that sets up the ghost scene.
new_text: The room was cold, because it rarely had a fire. It was silent, because it was far from the nursery and kitchen. It was solemn, because everyone knew how rarely it was entered. Only the housemaid came here on Saturdays to dust the mirrors and furniture. And Mrs. Reed herself, at long intervals, visited it to check the contents of a secret drawer in the wardrobe, where she kept various documents, her jewelry box, and a portrait of her dead husband. In those last words lies the secret of the red room—the spell that kept it so lonely despite its grandeur.

problem: In the list "sanguine, brilliant, careless, exacting, handsome, romping child", "exacting" is mistranslated as "bold" and "romping" is dropped.
new_text: I was a misfit at Gateshead Hall. I was unlike anyone there. I had nothing in common with Mrs. Reed or her children or her chosen household. If they didn't love me, I loved them just as little. They had no reason to feel affection for someone who couldn't relate to any of them—an outsider, different in temperament, ability, and inclination. A useless thing, unable to serve their interests or add to their pleasure. A troublesome thing, harboring the seeds of resentment at their treatment and contempt for their judgment. I know that if I had been a cheerful, bright, carefree, demanding, pretty, boisterous child—though equally dependent and friendless—Mrs. Reed would have tolerated my presence more easily. Her children would have felt more warmth toward me. The servants would have been less inclined to make me the nursery scapegoat.

problem: Dead men returning "to punish the perjured and avenge the oppressed" became "protect the wronged" — vengeance is the point of Jane's fear.
new_text: A strange idea occurred to me. I had never doubted that if Mr. Reed had been alive, he would have treated me kindly. And now, as I sat staring at the white bed and shadowed walls—glancing now and then at the dimly glinting mirror—I began to recall what I'd heard about dead men, disturbed in their graves when their last wishes were violated, returning to earth to punish oath-breakers and avenge the wronged. I imagined Mr. Reed's spirit, troubled by the suffering of his sister's child, might leave its resting place—whether in the church vault or wherever the dead go—and appear before me in this room. I wiped my tears and stifled my sobs, afraid that any sign of violent grief might summon a supernatural voice to comfort me, or draw from the shadows some glowing face bending over me with unearthly pity. This idea, comforting in theory, would have been terrifying in reality, and I tried with all my strength to suppress it. I tried to be brave. Shaking my hair from my eyes, I raised my head and forced myself to look boldly around the dark room. At that moment, a light gleamed on the wall. Was it, I wondered, a ray of moonlight coming through a gap in the blind? No—moonlight would be steady, and this was moving. As I watched, it glided up to the ceiling and flickered above my head. I can easily guess now that the light was probably from a lantern carried by someone crossing the lawn. But at the time, with my mind primed for horror and my nerves shattered, I thought the darting beam was a sign of some approaching vision from another world. My heart pounded, my head burned. A sound filled my ears that I took for the rushing of wings. Something seemed near me. I felt crushed, suffocated. My endurance broke. I rushed to the door and shook the lock in desperate effort. Footsteps came running along the hallway outside. The key turned. Bessie and Abbot entered.

problem: "a precocious actress" became "a dramatic little actress" — "precocious" (acting beyond her years, i.e. calculated) is lost.
new_text: "Silence! This behavior is utterly revolting." And no doubt she believed it. In her eyes, I was a precocious little actress. She genuinely saw me as a bundle of violent passions, petty spirit, and dangerous deceit.

problem: "You fell sick ... with crying" became "You fainted" — Bessie's vaguer diagnosis is made specific.
new_text: "You made yourself ill, I suppose, in the red room from all the crying. You'll be better soon, I'm sure."

problem: Bessie's "I wonder if she saw anything." is dropped — it is the line that prompts the ghost gossip in 3.15–3.16.
new_text: "Sarah, come sleep with me in the nursery. I'm terrified to be alone with that poor child tonight. She could die. It's so strange that she had that fit. I wonder if she saw anything. The Missus was rather too hard on her."

problem: The biblical echo "for you knew not what you did" (Luke 23:34) is flattened to "you didn't know what you were doing", and "uprooting my bad propensities" loses its image as "correcting".
new_text: No serious or lasting physical illness followed the red room incident. It only gave my nerves a shock whose aftershocks I feel to this day. Yes, Mrs. Reed, I owe you some terrible moments of mental anguish. But I should forgive you, for you knew not what you did. While you were tearing my heart apart, you thought you were only rooting out my bad tendencies.

problem: "a wreath of convolvuli and rosebuds" reduced to "a wreath of flowers"; and the source's spelling "Brobdignag" silently changed to "Brobdingnag" (proper nouns are to be kept as in the source).
new_text: Bessie had been down to the kitchen and brought back a tart on a certain brightly painted china plate, whose bird of paradise nestled in a wreath of morning glories and rosebuds. That plate had always stirred in me a rush of admiration, and I had often begged to be allowed to hold it and examine it up close, but had always been considered unworthy of such a privilege. Now this precious dish was placed on my knee, and I was warmly invited to eat the ring of delicate pastry on it. But it was no use. Like most long-awaited favors, it came too late. I couldn't eat the tart, and the plumage of the bird, the colors of the flowers, seemed strangely faded. I pushed both plate and tart away. Bessie asked if I wanted a book. The word book acted as a brief spark, and I asked her to fetch Gulliver's Travels from the library. I had read that book again and again with delight. I considered it a true account and found in it a deeper interest than fairy tales offered. As for elves, having searched for them in vain among foxglove leaves and bells, under mushrooms, and beneath the ivy on old walls, I had finally accepted the sad truth that they had all left England for some wild country where the forests were thicker and the people fewer. But Lilliput and Brobdignag, I firmly believed, were real places on the earth's surface, and I had no doubt that someday, by taking a long voyage, I would see with my own eyes the tiny fields, houses, and trees, the miniature people, the little cows, sheep, and birds of one realm, and the towering crops, the enormous dogs, the monstrous cats, and the giant men and women of the other. Yet now, when this beloved book was placed in my hands—when I turned its pages and looked for the magic in its wonderful pictures that had never failed me before—everything was eerie and bleak. The giants were gaunt goblins, the little people were sinister imps, and Gulliver was the loneliest wanderer in the most terrifying of lands. I closed the book, afraid to keep reading, and put it on the table beside the untouched tart.

problem: "I was doing very well" became "doing well enough", weakening Bessie's report (which Lloyd then contrasts with Jane's unhappy look).
new_text: Bessie said I was doing very well.

problem: "Having considered me at leisure" became "for a moment" — the reverse of his unhurried scrutiny.
new_text: The kind apothecary looked a little puzzled. I was standing before him, and he studied me steadily. His eyes were small and gray, not especially bright, but I think now they were quite shrewd. He had a rough-featured but kind-looking face. After considering me at his leisure, he said—

problem: Lloyd's jocular "I'll give Miss Jane a lecture till you come back" became "have a talk", losing his teasing tone.
new_text: As he tucked the box back into his waistcoat pocket, a loud bell rang for the servants' dinner. He knew what it was. "That's for you, nurse," he said. "You can go down. I'll give Miss Jane a lecture till you come back."

problem: "a beggarly set" became "a wretched lot", breaking the link to Jane's next words "I should not like to go a begging".
new_text: "I can't say. Aunt Reed says if I have any, they must be a beggarly lot. I wouldn't want to go begging."

problem: "sat in the stocks" (a posture-training device) became "sat on hard benches", which changes the image.
new_text: I thought again. I barely knew what school was. Bessie sometimes described it as a place where young ladies sat with their feet held in stocks, wore stiff boards strapped to their backs for posture, and were expected to be extremely refined and proper. John Reed hated his school and complained about his teachers—but John Reed's tastes were no guide for mine. And if Bessie's accounts of school discipline (gathered from the young ladies of a family where she had worked before Gateshead) were somewhat alarming, her descriptions of the skills those same young ladies had acquired were, I thought, equally appealing. She boasted of beautiful landscape and flower paintings they had done, songs they could sing and pieces they could play, purses they could knit, French books they could translate. My spirit stirred with ambition as I listened. Besides, school would be a complete change. It would mean a long journey, a total separation from Gateshead, and entry into a new life.

problem: Abbot's hedges are dropped: "Missis was, she dared say, glad enough" and "who always looked as if she were watching everybody" became flat assertions ("was always watching everybody").
new_text: Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way out. In the conversation that followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I gathered from what happened afterward that the apothecary suggested I be sent to school. The suggestion was no doubt eagerly accepted, because as Abbot said when discussing it with Bessie one night while they sewed in the nursery—after I was in bed and, they assumed, asleep—"The Missus was, I dare say, glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-natured child, who always looked as if she were watching everybody and scheming behind their backs." Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infant Guy Fawkes.

problem: Abbot's insult "such a little toad as that" became "such an ugly little creature", losing her memorable image.
new_text: "Yes," Abbot replied. "If she were a nice, pretty child, you might feel sorry for her being alone in the world. But you really can't care much about such a little toad as that."
